entries.title: Check your Node.js version
entries.when_to_use: When an npm-installed tool fails, to confirm Node is installed and recent.
entries.explanation:
Prints the installed Node.js version. Many command-line tools need a recent Node.
If Node itself isn't found, that's the first thing to fix.

expect.meaning: Node.js is installed; this is its version.
Node.js isn't installed or isn't on PATH.

entries.title: Find where npm installs global tools
entries.when_to_use: When a globally installed npm tool isn't found.
entries.explanation:
Prints the folder npm installs "global" tools into. On Linux the tools go in its bin
subfolder; on Windows directly in it. If that folder isn't on PATH, your terminal can't
find the tools.

expect.meaning: npm installs tools under your home folder.
npm installs tools in a system folder.
npm installs tools in your Windows user folder.
npm isn't installed or isn't on PATH.

entries.title: Try the tool again in a new terminal
manual_steps: Close all terminal windows and open a new one.
Run the tool the way you did before.
Tell me whether it works now.
entries.when_to_use: After a PATH change, or when the tool is found but still failing.
entries.explanation: Terminals read PATH when they start, so changes only show up in new terminal windows. Close and reopen yours to pick up the fix.

entries.title: Restart your computer
manual_steps: Save your work and close your apps.
Restart the computer (not Shut down; Restart).
Come back to this page afterwards. Your session will still be here.
entries.when_to_use: When a driver is stuck or an update needs a restart.
entries.explanation: A restart reloads every driver and service from scratch. It fixes stuck hardware more reliably than any command.

entries.title: Restart your router
manual_steps: Unplug the router's power cable (and the modem's, if separate).
Wait 30 seconds, then plug them back in.
Wait about 2 minutes for the lights to settle, then reconnect to Wi-Fi.
Tell me whether websites load now.
entries.when_to_use: When the computer looks fine but the router isn't handing out addresses or DNS.
entries.explanation: Routers get stuck like any computer. A restart clears their memory and usually fixes address and DNS problems for every device at home.

entries.title: Check if Bluetooth is blocked
entries.when_to_use: First check for any Bluetooth problem on Linux.
entries.explanation:
Linux can switch radios off in software ("soft block") or through a physical switch or
BIOS setting ("hard block"). This lists the Bluetooth radios the system knows about and
whether either block is on. It only reads status.

expect.meaning: Bluetooth is switched off in software. We can switch it back on.
A physical switch, function key or BIOS setting is turning Bluetooth off.
Nothing is blocking Bluetooth.
No Bluetooth radio was found at all.

entries.title: Switch Bluetooth back on (remove the software block)
entries.when_to_use: When rfkill shows "Soft blocked: yes" for Bluetooth.
entries.explanation:
Removes the software block that is keeping the Bluetooth radio off. It is the same as
flipping Bluetooth back on, just more direct. It asks for your password because it
changes a system setting. It prints nothing when it works.

expect.meaning: No output means it worked.
It needs administrator rights; make sure sudo is at the start.

entries.title: Check the Bluetooth service
entries.when_to_use: When nothing blocks Bluetooth but it still doesn't work.
entries.explanation:
Bluetooth on Linux needs a background program (the bluetooth service, part of BlueZ)
to be running. This shows whether it is running, stopped, or not installed, plus its
last few log lines. It only reads status.

expect.meaning: The Bluetooth service is running.
The Bluetooth service is stopped.
The service is set not to start when the computer boots.
The Bluetooth service (BlueZ) doesn't seem to be installed.

entries.title: Start the Bluetooth service and keep it on at boot
entries.when_to_use: When the bluetooth service is stopped or disabled.
entries.explanation:
Starts the Bluetooth service now and sets it to start automatically every time the
computer boots. Without it running, no Bluetooth device can connect.

expect.meaning: It worked.
The service failed to start; the logs will say why.

entries.title: Restart the Bluetooth service
entries.when_to_use: When the service runs but devices won't connect or the adapter seems stuck.
entries.explanation:
Stops and starts the Bluetooth service, like turning it off and on again. Connected
Bluetooth devices disconnect for a few seconds and usually reconnect on their own.

expect.meaning: No output means it restarted.

entries.undo: n/a — restarts the service; devices reconnect on their own

entries.title: Check the Bluetooth adapter is powered on
entries.when_to_use: After the service is running, to see if the adapter is detected and powered.

expect.meaning: The adapter is on.
The adapter is detected but switched off.
The Bluetooth service can't see any adapter.
The Bluetooth service isn't running.

entries.title: Power on the Bluetooth adapter
entries.when_to_use: When bluetoothctl show says "Powered: no".
entries.explanation:
Tells the Bluetooth service to switch the adapter on. It's the same as the Bluetooth
toggle in Settings. If something is blocking the radio, it will say so.

expect.meaning: The adapter is now on.
Something is blocking the radio.

entries.title: Look for the Bluetooth hardware
entries.when_to_use: When no Bluetooth adapter is detected at all.
entries.explanation:
Most laptop Bluetooth chips are connected over USB inside the machine. This lists USB
devices and keeps only lines that mention Bluetooth or wireless. An empty result means
the system can't see the chip, which points to hardware, BIOS settings or drivers.

expect.meaning: The Bluetooth hardware is visible to the system.
No Bluetooth hardware is visible over USB.

entries.title: Check the system log for Bluetooth driver errors
entries.when_to_use: When the adapter is missing or behaves oddly, to find driver or firmware errors.
entries.explanation:
The kernel keeps a log of hardware events since boot. This shows only the lines about
Bluetooth, its USB driver (btusb) and firmware. Missing firmware or timeouts show up
here. It needs your password because the kernel log is restricted on Ubuntu.

expect.pattern: firmware.*(not found|failed|error)|Failed to load firmware|direct firmware load .* failed
expect.meaning: The Bluetooth chip's firmware didn't load.
The adapter isn't responding to the driver.

when.output_matches: firmware.*(not found|failed|error)|Failed to load firmware|direct firmware load .* failed

entries.title: Read the Bluetooth service log
entries.when_to_use: When the service runs but something still fails and we need its error messages.
entries.explanation:
Shows the last 50 log lines from the Bluetooth service since this boot. Error messages
here usually name the exact problem, such as a failed setting or a device refusing to pair.

expect.meaning: There are errors worth reading in these lines.

entries.title: Reload the Bluetooth USB driver
entries.command: sudo modprobe -r btusb && sudo modprobe btusb
entries.when_to_use: When the adapter times out or is stuck, and restarting the service didn't help.
entries.explanation:
Unloads the Bluetooth USB driver and loads it again, like unplugging and replugging the
chip. All Bluetooth devices disconnect. If it says the module is in use, a restart of
the computer does the same thing more reliably.

expect.meaning: The driver reloaded.
The driver is busy; restart the computer instead.

entries.undo: If Bluetooth stays missing, restart the computer; the driver loads again at boot.

entries.title: Check that BlueZ (the Bluetooth software) is installed
entries.when_to_use: When the bluetooth service can't be found.
entries.explanation:
Asks the package manager whether BlueZ, the standard Linux Bluetooth software, is
installed, and which version. It only reads the package database.

expect.meaning: BlueZ is installed.
BlueZ is not installed.

entries.title: Install BlueZ from Ubuntu's official packages
entries.when_to_use: When dpkg says bluez is not installed.
entries.explanation:
Installs BlueZ from your distribution's official, signed package repositories. It asks
you to confirm before installing. It downloads only from the same place your normal
system updates come from.

expect.pattern: Setting up bluez|is already the newest version
expect.meaning: BlueZ is installed.

entries.title: Turn off the hardware switch for wireless
manual_steps: Look for a key with an antenna or airplane icon, often Fn plus one of F2–F12, and press it once.
Check the sides of the laptop for a small wireless on/off switch.
If neither exists, the block may be a BIOS/UEFI setting. That's a job for a person, so tell me if the key didn't help.
entries.when_to_use: When rfkill shows "Hard blocked: yes".
entries.explanation:
A hard block is set by hardware, a function key or the BIOS, not by Linux, so no command
can remove it. Pressing the wireless key or flipping the switch is the usual fix.
entries.undo: Press the same key or flip the switch back.

entries.title: Try connecting your Bluetooth device now
manual_steps: Open Settings → Bluetooth and make sure Bluetooth is on.
Put your device (headphones, mouse…) in pairing mode.
Select it in the list and connect. If it was paired before and won't connect, click it and choose "Remove Device", then pair again.
entries.when_to_use: After the adapter is on, to check if the original problem is fixed.
entries.explanation:
Now that the adapter is working, this checks the thing you actually care about:
connecting your device. Removing and re-pairing clears old pairing data that often
breaks after updates.

entries.title: Find where a command-line tool is installed

tool.description: The tool that says "command not found"

entries.when_to_use: First check when a tool says "command not found".
entries.explanation:
Asks your shell where it finds this tool. If it prints a path, the shell can find it.
If it prints nothing, the tool is either not installed or installed in a folder your
shell doesn't search (your PATH).

expect.meaning: The shell finds the tool at this path.
The shell can't find the tool.

entries.title: List the folders your shell searches (PATH)
entries.when_to_use: To check whether a tool's install folder is on PATH.
entries.explanation:
Your shell looks for commands only in the folders listed in PATH. This prints them one
per line so we can see whether the folder your tool was installed into is missing.

expect.meaning: A user-level tools folder is on your PATH.

entries.title: Add npm's global tools folder to PATH

prefix_path.description: npm prefix from the previous step, e.g. $HOME/.npm-global

rc_file.description: Your shell's startup file (bash or zsh)

entries.when_to_use: When npm's prefix is under $HOME and its bin folder is missing from PATH.
entries.explanation:
Adds one line to your shell's startup file so every new terminal also searches npm's
global tools folder. It doesn't install or delete anything. Run it once only; running
it twice adds a duplicate line (harmless but untidy). Open a new terminal afterwards.

expect.meaning: The line was added. Open a new terminal window next.

entries.undo: Open the file (e.g. ~/.bashrc) in a text editor and delete the last line that starts with export PATH=

sources.title: npm Docs — Resolving EACCES permissions errors

entries.title: Show your Linux version
entries.when_to_use: When the Linux distribution or version is unknown.
entries.explanation:
Prints a small text file every modern Linux system has, which names the distribution
and its version. Different versions ship different Bluetooth and network tools, so this
helps pick the right steps. It only reads a file.

expect.meaning: The line starting with PRETTY_NAME is your distribution and version.

entries.title: Show your kernel version
entries.when_to_use: When a driver or firmware problem is suspected and the kernel version matters.
entries.explanation:
Prints the version of the Linux kernel you are running. Drivers for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
live in the kernel, so some problems only affect certain versions. It changes nothing.

expect.meaning: This is your kernel version.

entries.title: Check if Wi-Fi is switched on
entries.when_to_use: First check for Wi-Fi problems on Linux with NetworkManager (Ubuntu default).
entries.explanation:
Asks NetworkManager, the program that manages networks on Ubuntu, whether the Wi-Fi
radio is enabled. It prints one word and changes nothing.

expect.meaning: Wi-Fi is switched on.
Wi-Fi is switched off.
NetworkManager isn't installed; this machine manages networks differently.

entries.title: Switch Wi-Fi on
entries.when_to_use: When nmcli says Wi-Fi is disabled.
entries.explanation:
Turns the Wi-Fi radio on, the same as the Wi-Fi toggle in Settings. It prints nothing
when it works. If a hardware switch is off, it won't be able to turn it on.

expect.meaning: No output means it worked.

entries.title: See the state of your Wi-Fi adapter
entries.when_to_use: To see whether the Wi-Fi adapter exists and whether it's connected.
entries.explanation:
Lists your network adapters and their state: connected, disconnected, or unavailable.
"Unavailable" usually means the radio is blocked or the driver has a problem.

expect.meaning: Wi-Fi is connected to a network.
Wi-Fi works but isn't connected to a network.
The Wi-Fi adapter is blocked or not ready.

entries.title: Check if Wi-Fi is blocked
entries.when_to_use: When the Wi-Fi adapter is unavailable.
entries.explanation:
Shows whether the Wi-Fi radio is blocked in software or by a hardware switch. It only
reads status.

expect.meaning: Wi-Fi is switched off in software.
A hardware switch or key is turning Wi-Fi off.

entries.title: Remove the software block on Wi-Fi
entries.when_to_use: When rfkill shows Wi-Fi "Soft blocked: yes".
entries.explanation:
Removes the software block that keeps the Wi-Fi radio off. It asks for your password
because it changes a system setting.

expect.meaning: No output means it worked.

entries.title: Turn off the hardware switch for Wi-Fi
manual_steps: Press the key with an antenna or airplane icon (often Fn plus one of F2–F12).
Check the laptop's sides for a wireless switch.
Tell me if that changed anything.
entries.when_to_use: When Wi-Fi is hard blocked.
entries.explanation:
A hard block comes from hardware or firmware, so software can't lift it. The wireless
key or switch usually can.
entries.undo: Press the key or flip the switch back.

entries.title: Connect to your Wi-Fi network
manual_steps: Click the network icon in the top-right corner and open Wi-Fi.
Pick your network and enter its password. Type it there, never in this chat.
Tell me whether it connected.
entries.when_to_use: When Wi-Fi works but is disconnected.
entries.explanation:
The adapter is fine but not joined to a network. Connecting through Settings is the
simplest way and keeps your Wi-Fi password on your computer.

entries.title: Check your network addresses
entries.when_to_use: When connected but nothing loads, to see if the router gave you an address.
entries.explanation:
Lists each network adapter with its IP address. A normal home address looks like
192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x. An address starting with 169.254 means the router never
answered.

expect.meaning: Your Wi-Fi has a normal local address.
The router didn't give you an address.

entries.title: Check the route to the internet
entries.when_to_use: When you have an address but can't reach the internet.
entries.explanation:
Shows where your computer sends traffic. A line starting with "default via" is the
route to the internet through your router. Without it, nothing outside your home
network loads.

expect.meaning: There's a route to the internet.

entries.title: Test the internet connection by address
entries.when_to_use: To tell apart "no internet" from "names don't resolve".
entries.explanation:
Sends four small test messages to a well-known public server by its number, skipping
name lookup. If these get answers, your internet works and the problem is likely DNS
(turning names into addresses).

expect.meaning: The internet is reachable.
The internet isn't reachable at all.

entries.title: Test that website names resolve (DNS)
entries.when_to_use: When the internet works by address but websites don't load.
entries.explanation:
Asks your system to turn a website name into an address, which is what DNS does. If
nothing prints, name lookup is broken, which makes it look like the internet is down.

expect.meaning: Name lookup works.
Name lookup is failing.

entries.title: See which DNS servers you're using
entries.when_to_use: When DNS fails, to see which DNS servers are configured.
entries.explanation:
Shows the DNS servers each network adapter uses. Usually it's your router's address.
If none are listed for Wi-Fi, name lookup can't work.

expect.meaning: DNS servers are configured.

entries.title: Clear the DNS cache
entries.when_to_use: When name lookup fails or returns stale results.
entries.explanation:
Clears the list of recently looked-up website addresses that your computer keeps. A
stale or broken entry can stop sites loading. The list rebuilds itself automatically.

expect.meaning: The cache was cleared.

entries.title: Test name lookup again
entries.when_to_use: After clearing the DNS cache, to see if it helped.
entries.explanation: Same test as before. If a name and address print now, clearing the cache fixed it.

expect.meaning: Name lookup works now.
Still failing.

entries.title: Restart NetworkManager
entries.when_to_use: When the adapter is fine but connections fail or hang.
entries.explanation:
Restarts the program that manages your network connections. Your connection drops for
a few seconds and should come back by itself.

expect.meaning: It restarted.

entries.undo: n/a — restarts the service; Wi-Fi reconnects on its own

entries.title: Try loading a website
manual_steps: Open a new browser tab and load a site you use often.
Tell me whether it loads.
entries.when_to_use: After network tests pass, to confirm the original problem is fixed.
entries.explanation: This checks the thing you actually care about, not just a test command. If the site loads, your connection is fixed.

entries.title: List Bluetooth devices and their status
entries.when_to_use: First check for any Bluetooth problem on Windows.
entries.explanation:
Lists every Bluetooth item Windows knows about and its status. "OK" means working,
"Error" means a driver problem, and "Unknown" means the device isn't present right now.
It only reads information.

expect.meaning: A Bluetooth device has a driver problem.
These items are working.
These items aren't present right now (often old or disconnected devices).
Windows can't see any Bluetooth hardware.

entries.title: Check the Bluetooth Support Service
entries.command: Get-Service bthserv | Format-List Name, Status, StartType
entries.when_to_use: When Bluetooth devices show errors or won't connect.
entries.explanation:
Windows needs the "Bluetooth Support Service" (bthserv) for Bluetooth to work. This
shows whether it's running and how it starts. It only reads status.

expect.meaning: The service is running.
The service is stopped.
The service is disabled and can't start.

entries.title: Allow the Bluetooth service to start
entries.when_to_use: When bthserv is Disabled.
entries.explanation:
Changes the Bluetooth Support Service from "Disabled" back to Windows' default
("Manual"), so it can start when needed. Run it in a terminal opened as administrator.

expect.meaning: It worked.
The terminal isn't running as administrator.

entries.title: Start the Bluetooth service
entries.when_to_use: When bthserv is stopped.
entries.explanation: Starts the Bluetooth Support Service now. Run it in a terminal opened as administrator.

expect.meaning: The service started.
Windows couldn't start it, often a permissions or driver problem.

entries.title: Restart the Bluetooth service
entries.when_to_use: When the service runs but Bluetooth is stuck or devices error.
entries.explanation:
Stops and starts the Bluetooth Support Service. Connected Bluetooth devices drop for a
few seconds. Run it in a terminal opened as administrator.

expect.meaning: It restarted.

entries.title: Check Airplane mode and the Bluetooth toggle
manual_steps: Press Windows + A to open Quick Settings.
Make sure Airplane mode is off and Bluetooth is on.
If there's no Bluetooth button at all, tell me. That usually means a driver problem.
entries.when_to_use: When Windows sees no Bluetooth hardware, or as a first quick check.
entries.explanation: Airplane mode turns off every radio, including Bluetooth. It's the most common cause and takes five seconds to check.

entries.title: Look for a Bluetooth driver update
manual_steps: Open Settings → Windows Update → Advanced options → Optional updates.
Open "Driver updates". If you see a Bluetooth or wireless driver, select it and install.
Restart the computer if Windows asks, then come back here.
entries.when_to_use: When a Bluetooth device shows Error or the service won't start.
entries.explanation: Windows Update offers tested drivers from your laptop's maker. A newer driver often fixes a Bluetooth adapter that shows an error.
entries.undo: Settings → Windows Update → Update history → Uninstall updates (for drivers: Device Manager → Roll back driver).

entries.title: Try connecting your Bluetooth device now
manual_steps: Open Settings → Bluetooth & devices.
Put your device in pairing mode, then click "Add device" and pick it.
If it was paired before and won't connect, open it and choose "Remove device", then add it again.
entries.when_to_use: After Bluetooth is back on, to check the original problem is fixed.
entries.explanation: This checks what you actually care about. Removing and re-adding clears old pairing data that often breaks after updates.

entries.title: Find where a command-line tool is installed
entries.when_to_use: First check when a tool is "not recognized as a command".
entries.explanation:
Asks Windows where it finds this tool. We use where.exe because in PowerShell plain
"where" means something else. A path means Windows finds it; "Could not find" means
it's not installed or not on PATH.

expect.meaning: Windows can't find the tool on PATH.
Windows finds the tool at this path.

entries.title: List the folders Windows searches (PATH)
entries.when_to_use: To check whether npm's folder is on PATH.
entries.explanation:
Windows looks for commands only in the folders listed in PATH. This prints them one per
line so we can see whether npm's folder is missing.

expect.meaning: npm's folder is on your PATH.

entries.title: Add npm's folder to your PATH (Windows settings)
manual_steps: Press Start, type "environment variables" and open "Edit environment variables for your account".
In the top list, select Path and click Edit.
Click New and paste the folder from the npm step (usually %APPDATA%\npm).
Click OK on every window, then close and reopen your terminal.
entries.when_to_use: When npm's Windows folder isn't on PATH.
entries.explanation: This adds npm's folder to the list Windows searches for commands, only for your account. Nothing is installed or deleted.
entries.undo: Open the same window, select that Path entry and click Delete.

entries.title: Show your Windows version
entries.when_to_use: When the Windows version or build is unknown.
entries.explanation:
Shows your Windows edition, version and build number. It can take a few seconds.
Some fixes depend on the build. It only reads information.

expect.meaning: You're on Windows 11.
You're on Windows 10.

entries.title: Check your Wi-Fi connection details
entries.when_to_use: First check for Wi-Fi problems on Windows.
entries.explanation:
Shows your Wi-Fi adapter, whether it's connected, to which network, and the signal
strength. It only reads information. On newer Windows 11 builds it may ask for
Location permission, because Wi-Fi details can reveal where you are.

expect.meaning: Wi-Fi is connected.
Wi-Fi isn't connected to a network.
Windows can't see a Wi-Fi adapter.
Windows wants Location permission to show Wi-Fi details.

entries.title: List network adapters
entries.when_to_use: When Wi-Fi seems missing or disabled.
entries.explanation:
Lists your network adapters (Wi-Fi, Ethernet) and whether each is Up, Disconnected or
Disabled. It only reads information.

expect.meaning: The Wi-Fi adapter is turned off in Windows.
The Wi-Fi adapter is on and connected.

entries.title: Turn the Wi-Fi adapter back on

adapter.description: Adapter name from the list, e.g. Wi-Fi

entries.when_to_use: When the Wi-Fi adapter shows Disabled.
entries.explanation:
Re-enables the Wi-Fi adapter Windows had switched off. Run it in a terminal opened as
administrator.

expect.meaning: The adapter is enabled.

entries.title: Connect to your Wi-Fi network
manual_steps: Click the network icon on the taskbar and open the Wi-Fi list (the arrow next to Wi-Fi).
Pick your network and enter its password. Type it there, never in this chat.
Tell me whether it connected.
entries.when_to_use: When Wi-Fi is on but disconnected.
entries.explanation: Your adapter works but isn't joined to a network. Joining through Windows keeps the password on your PC.

entries.title: Test the internet connection by address
entries.when_to_use: To tell apart "no internet" from "names don't resolve".
entries.explanation:
Sends four small test messages to a well-known public server by its number, skipping
name lookup. Answers mean your internet works and the problem is probably DNS.

expect.meaning: The internet is reachable.
The internet isn't reachable.

entries.title: Test that website names resolve (DNS)
entries.when_to_use: When the internet works by address but websites don't load.
entries.explanation:
Asks Windows to turn a website name into an address (DNS). If this fails while the
address test worked, DNS is the problem.

expect.meaning: Name lookup works.

expect.pattern: DNS name does not exist|timeout period expired|DNS server failure|not found
expect.meaning: Name lookup is failing.

when.output_matches: DNS name does not exist|timeout period expired|DNS server failure|not found

entries.title: Clear the DNS cache
entries.when_to_use: When name lookup fails or returns stale results.
entries.explanation:
Clears Windows' list of recently looked-up website addresses. A stale entry can stop
sites loading. The list rebuilds itself automatically.

expect.meaning: The cache was cleared.
Run it in a terminal opened as administrator.

entries.title: Test name lookup again
entries.when_to_use: After clearing the DNS cache.
entries.explanation: Same test as before. If a name and address print now, clearing the DNS cache fixed the problem.

expect.meaning: Name lookup works now.

entries.title: Restart the Wi-Fi adapter
entries.when_to_use: When the adapter is up but connections keep failing.
entries.explanation:
Turns the Wi-Fi adapter off and on. Your connection drops for a few seconds. Run it in
a terminal opened as administrator.

expect.meaning: The adapter restarted.

entries.undo: n/a — the adapter comes back on by itself

entries.title: Try loading a website
manual_steps: Open a new browser tab and load a site you use often.
Tell me whether it loads.
entries.when_to_use: After network tests pass, to confirm the original problem is fixed.
entries.explanation: This checks the thing you care about, not just a test. If a normal site loads, your connection is working again.
